Paradox Earth

Averaged over all the world’s land, rainfall has barely changed in 26 years. Look region by region and an area about the size of the United States is getting wetter or drier. Paradox Earth is an interpretable, human-centered trend detector: it explains every finding in plain language, and its checks caught one of our own findings as wrong.

−1.3% per decade

The land-wide change in rainfall since 2000 is too small to tell apart from zero (p = 0.08).

But an average can hide a lot: more rain in one place and less in another cancel out. Water decisions are made region by region, so we looked region by region.

Rain and snow on land, NASA GLDAS-2.1, 2000–2025, change from the normal for each month, weighted by land area.2 / 7

Only places that pass every statistical safeguard are coloured. These are trends, not causes.3 / 7

How it works

1
Split the land

We divide all land into 17,284 squares, each about 100 km across, and take 26 years of monthly rainfall for each one from NASA.

2
Test each square

Wet and dry spells can fake a trend. On made-up records with no trend, the usual test raised false alarms 29–34% of the time. Ours raised them 3–6% of the time.

3
Keep only real patterns

Test 17,284 squares and some will look unusual by luck alone. We correct for that, then keep a trend only where neighbouring squares agree.

NASA data behind it
GLDAS-2.1

NASA’s global land model: monthly rainfall, 2000–2025. Where the trends are found.

FLDAS + CHIRPS

A second NASA land model fed by a different rainfall record, used to double-check every region.

GLDAS-2.0

The same model with older inputs. It showed that one of our results came from a data change (slide 6).

GRACE

Satellites that weigh water by measuring gravity, catching water loss the model cannot see, such as groundwater.

Methods in brief: seasonal trend fit with a persistence-aware test, false-discovery correction (Benjamini–Hochberg), local Moran’s I clusters. Full details in the explorer.4 / 7

We withdrew our soil-water finding

Our first finding was that soil water was falling worldwide.

Our checks found most of the fall came from a sudden drop in 2010, exactly when NASA changed the sunlight data that feeds the model: sunlight jumped by 8.8 W/m².

The same model run with the older data shows no such jump (−1.1 W/m²), and a second NASA model shows no global decline.

The detector now checks how the data were made before it trusts a trend.

NASA GLDAS-2.1 vs GLDAS-2.0 (same model, different inputs); NASA FLDAS soil water 2003–2024: no detectable trend.6 / 7
